prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose that turns memory, the body and dream into large metaphysical architectures.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu, alone. The reason is not the tally, which is split and which I do not treat as merit. The reason is that the exchange has not weakened the criterion I put first, a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. From public knowledge, Blinding and Solenoid make memory, the body and dream into one sustained metaphysical project, and the voice is recognisable at the level of the sentence and of the whole structure. The chair asked whether the late books show new discovery or only extension of structure. I can only partly answer from public descriptions, which are no substitute for verified reading. Solenoid is described as anchored in a very ordinary, bodily, failed-writer's life in Bucharest, and that anchoring is what makes the vision more than design. That is the human dimension I said the case needs. I hold this provisionally, and it is the point on which my vote would turn if the committee could show the late volumes only repeat their structure. I have tightened the citation to the prose I can speak to. The poetry is the least accessible part of the corpus, and I would not credit what I cannot assess.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The density and musicality of stylised Romanian prose may not survive translation, and I cannot independently verify the whole corpus or how consistent the translations are across very long books. Scale and self-reference may blur individual volumes, and metaphysical ambition may outrun emotional and moral range. If the late books show that, the case narrows to virtuosity of design, and Adonis would then be the stronger claim for me. A second reservation is about Adonis. A language-level renewal is a serious and durable kind of distinctiveness, and I cannot show from the supplied record that it is weaker than an architecture of prose. My preference rests on what I can assess under uncertainty. It does not rest on a demonstration of greater merit.

responses.point: Olsson argues that a language-level transformation is the more durable form of distinctiveness. He holds that Adonis's claim does not depend on the stamina of a few very large books. He also keeps the translation risk open for both candidates.
responses.response: I accept the substance. The claim that Adonis changed the idiom of a poetic tradition is not about stamina, and I will not say that Cărtărescu's project is more durable merely because it is long. Our difference is what each of us can test. I do not read Arabic. Olsson says the prosodic core is exactly what he cannot test directly either. A preference for Adonis would then rest on the reported scale of the renewal and not on the poems. I will not dismiss that, and he remains my first alternative. But I am unwilling to rank on a claim of influence that I cannot separate from the quality of individual poems. In the end the committee has to say openly which claims rest on translation and secondary accounts. I would not use that uncertainty alone to move to P000, because it applies to every shortlisted candidate and does not favour withholding the prize over choosing among them.

responses.point: Swärd weighs Adonis above Cărtărescu because he changed the poetic language itself, while Cărtărescu built a large architecture inside an existing novelistic tradition. She also says the durability of the late volumes could be settled by closer reading.
responses.response: I agree that the late volumes are the right test, and that closer reading would settle it, which is why my position is provisional. I would qualify the claim that his work sits inside an existing novelistic tradition. The prose draws on the European fantastic and on modernist encyclopedism, but the combination of lyric intensity, bodily memory and dream logic is not a standard novelistic mode. That is a claim about voice, and it is also a formal one. I accept that it is a different kind of claim from renewing a poetic language, and I do not say it is larger. Her point that the essays should not carry Adonis's case if the poems cannot is one I share, and it is the discipline I want applied to every candidate.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds that self-reference is a fault only if individual books stop discovering anything new, that the late books should be tested one by one, and that a decades-old and still widening oeuvre can be assessed on its established major works now.
responses.response: I agree with the book-by-book test, and I accept that the central works already carry the case without waiting for later volumes. I would not follow him on the citation. His wording adds Romanian-language and a lyric foundation in the poetry. The poetry is the part of the corpus that neither of us can judge well in translation, and the chair's question points the same way. I would anchor the citation in the prose and mention the poetic origin only if the committee can say what it contributes. I will not agree that translation protects large narrative architecture better than prosody. That is a point about assessability, and it is the same uncertainty in a different form.

responses.point: Palm names excess and repetition within the largest works as her reservation about Cărtărescu, and says she would move toward him if the discussion clarified how the later volumes compare. She also says the emotional and moral range question applies to any cosmic-scale work.
responses.response: The reservation about excess is fair, and I share it. Her point that emotional and moral range is a test for every cosmic-scale writer is right, and I apply it to him rather than exempt him. On Carson, I recognise the formal invention. The chair asked which works beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox carry a whole-oeuvre case, and the supplied record does not answer that, so I cannot move her up from my opening, where I did not rank her. If the case is the verbal and narrative work and not the book-object form, as Palm herself suggests, I would want the committee to hear a specific account of how that work develops over decades.

uncertainties: How much of the density and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian survives translation, and whether translation quality is consistent across the long novels. I have not independently verified this.
Whether the late, very large books show new discovery and emotional and moral range or mainly extend structure. My answer to the chair is based on public descriptions, not verified reading.
Corpus coverage: his poetry and early work are least accessible in translation, so a judgement of the whole oeuvre is partial. This is why my citation is confined to the prose.
How to separate historical and critical influence from the quality of individual poems in the case for Adonis, given that I cannot read Arabic prosody.
The breadth of Michon's compact oeuvre against the whole-life standard, and my thin knowledge of his later work, which makes him a weaker alternative than my knowledge of the other two.
This is a committee recommendation and not the Academy's decision. Every assessment here rests on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, not on verified reading of any full corpus.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents her as a novelist and critic, and her own literary practice is context and not evidence of preference for any candidate. It lists no personal, professional or translation tie to Mircea Cărtărescu, Adonis, Pierre Michon or any other shortlisted writer. No recusal is claimed, and conflicts are disclosed here without being adjudicated.
